For even Origen, whom they cite as their authority, plainly indicates the contrary—that "the land of Britain, before the coming of Christ," had by no means assented "to the religion of the one God"; indeed, Dio Cassius records by name that Andraste, or Andate, the goddess of Victory, and others record that Apollo and Diana, were customarily worshipped by the Britons. And concerning their idol-madness Gildas, their own countryman, bears testimony so clear that the matter ought not to be called into question. For thus he writes: "Therefore, passing over those ancient errors, shared with all peoples, by which the whole human race was held fast bound before the coming of Christ in the flesh; and not enumerating the very diabolical monstrosities of my homeland, almost surpassing in number those of Egypt, some of which, with their still-misshapen features, within or outside the deserted walls, we behold stiffening in their accustomed fashion with grim countenances; nor crying out by name against the very mountains, or hills, or rivers, once destructive but now useful for human purposes, upon which divine honour was then heaped by a blind people, etc."—so that concerning the most wretched condition of those times, and the most happy condition of those that followed, blessed Jerome did not hesitate to declare, in the epitaph of Nepotian: "Where then were the men of the whole world, from India even to Britain, from the frozen region of the north even to the heats of the Atlantic ocean—peoples so innumerable, and the multitudes of so many nations? How varied in their tongues, in the fashion both of their dress and of their arms?"
